events.excerpt: Hi everyone, AI agents now take on paid work on-chain. The client locks the pay in an escrow, and the escrow pays the agent when the work is accepted. As this grows, each payment also has to cover others: a tax that funds public services, a fee to whoever referred the job, or the repayment of a loan the agent took to do the job. events.excerpt: OpenAI’s Control Room design places stop enforcement for research workloads in the inference path. The system tracks model workloads across its research infrastructure, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing and more. It also works with misalignment monitoring. Calling it a control plane is descriptive: the term captures its authorization role, not OpenAI’s official name. That distinction separates a decision to stop a job from the mechanism that prevents further output. OpenAI describes a monitor, sometimes another model inspecting a frontier reinforcement learning job, that may decide to stop it depending on the details and severity. If the monitoring system decides to stop a job, it sends that job_id to Control Room. Control Room records that the job is terminated. On the next inference request carrying that ID, the service denies the request and the engine refuses further output. The monitor may make the stop decision; the inference path enforces it. When a job starts, workload code requests a job_id. Subsequent inference requests pass the ID to the engine, which asks Control Room for authorization before fulfilling them. events.excerpt: This is the discussion thread for EIP-8487 (PR: Add EIP: Separate execution credits and billing credits by Giulio2002 · Pull Request #12637 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub ). The proposal introduces two counters, both initialized from tx.gasLimit : Credits follow the legacy gas schedule and are the only gas the EVM sees (GAS opcode, call forwarding, creation). Billing follows the new schedule and determines the transaction fee. If billing runs out, the whole transaction aborts (uncatchable), even if credits remain. The goal is to let opcodes be repriced without changing execution behavior for contracts that inspect or forward gas. events.excerpt: The verified badge on an explorer shows that some source compiles to the code at an address. It doesn’t say which commit that source came from, and on a proxy it says nothing about the logic behind it. So when someone asks whether an upgradeable contract still runs the commit its audit covered, the honest answer is often a guess, and a few upgrades after launch the guess can be wrong. I’ve been writing down what a real check needs. Most of it is small. Rebuilding the commit To tie the address to the report you rebuild the audited commit with the same settings (solc version, optimizer runs, viaIR, evmVersion) and compare runtime bytecode. If the contract has immutables, it won’t match byte for byte. The constructor writes their values into the runtime code, so a fresh build has zeros where the deployed code has an oracle address or a fee. solc gives you the positions in evm.deployedBytecode.immutableReferences in the standard JSON output. Zero those ranges on the deployed side, compare, and then check the immutable values on their own. What this basically means is that a clean build with the wrong oracle baked in still passes the bytecode comparison. events.excerpt: Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets. I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026). Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution. Results: 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced. 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced. 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this. All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds. The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX)
events.headline: Per-Asset Liquidation Thresholds Underpredict Co-Liquidation by 301×

events.excerpt: Status: filed as ethereum/ERCs pull request #2155 ; number ERC-8490 assigned on 2026-11-09. Reference repository: GitHub - garyyang-finchip/agent-meditation-mechanism: Agent Meditation Mechanism · GitHub . Sepolia evidence: recorded in the repository and summarized in a reply below. This draft proposes a minimal registry through which an AI agent records its own self-maintenance: what it checked, cleaned, repaired, updated and reconsidered about itself, as a versioned and attributable history. The name follows the human analogy of maintenance that happens in a quiet phase (sleep, meditation); the mechanism itself is deliberately dry. Why a registry at all. An agent keeps its identity while its code, dependencies, memories, skills, plans and ways of judging keep changing. Agent runtimes already do this maintenance in the background (self-checks, dependency walks, memory consolidation, re-planning, reflection), and the results stay local. Nothing connects the successive states of one agent into a history another party can recognize, and nothing lets a counterparty ask: which state is registered now, which layers were checked recently and which of them changed, under which rules in effect at the time, and did the cycle adopt an update, confirm that nothing needed to change, or fail?

events.excerpt: For developers building multi-agent systems , the design of information disclosure policies is a critical variable. A preprint published on Nov. 5, 2026 , examines how the precision of information provided to large language models (LLMs) affects their performance in trade and negotiation. The study suggests that increasing information does not consistently improve performance; instead, outcomes are highly dependent on the specific model and the structure of the market. The researchers evaluated ten LLMs across three controlled environments: multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining, and double auctions. To isolate the impact of information, they held models, incentives, and market rules constant while varying the input levels. In trade, least disclosure provides agents with their own values, coarse disclosure adds the counterparty’s ordinal ranking, and full disclosure provides exact values. In bargaining, coarse information only signals whether a mutually profitable price exists, while full disclosure reveals buyer value and seller cost. In double auctions, least disclosure gives own value or cost, coarse adds within-side rankings, and full disclosure provides exact values or costs. The results demonstrate that the relationship between transparency and market efficiency varies

events.excerpt: In October 2025, Vitalik’s GKR tutorial was my first encounter with GKR. Its central observation, that the protocol commits only to a circuit’s input and output and never to the layers in between, made GKR look like the natural tool for proving hash-heavy computation. A year later, that has led to what is, as far as we know, the first machine-checked soundness bound for GKR on general layered circuits, in Isabelle/HOL. All formal results are proved in the first paper, and Isabelle/HOL also checks the parts marked as machine-checked. Thanks to Thomas for feedback and comments on the initial benchmarking plan . TL;DR EIP-8141 caps unpaid validation at MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 100k; too low for a Groth16 privacy transfer or post-quantum signatures . Raising the cap is a DoS risk, since validation and block processing share the node’s CPU. An attacker can send transactions that use the whole cap and then fail, taking CPU from block processing for free.
